name: Metformin: what to expect when starting
headline: Metformin: what the NHS says to expect when starting it
summary: The NHS describes metformin as the usual first medicine for type 2 diabetes. Side effects are mostly stomach-related and often ease.
keyPoints: The NHS says metformin is usually the first medicine prescribed for type 2 diabetes, and that it is also used in gestational diabetes and PMOS.
Common side effects are stomach-related; the NHS says most ease after a couple of weeks, and taking tablets with food or slow-release tablets can help.
The NHS says long-term use can cause vitamin B12 deficiency, so a doctor may check B12 levels.
The NHS says illness with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever risks dehydration, and metformin may need pausing before surgery or scans using dye.
For missed doses or side effects, a pharmacist or GP can advise; NHS 111 for urgent worries; 999 for suspected lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis.

body.heading: What is metformin used for?
body.body: The NHS describes metformin as a medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes, and says it is usually the first choice prescribed for it. It can also be used for gestational diabetes (diabetes in pregnancy) and for polycystic ovary syndrome, which the NHS pages call PMOS. Clinicians generally start it when diet and exercise alone have not been enough to control blood sugar. The NHS says it works by helping the body respond better to insulin and by reducing the sugar the liver releases into the blood. It is only available with a prescription.

body.heading: How is metformin taken?
body.body: The NHS says metformin comes as two kinds of tablet: standard tablets and slow-release (modified-release) tablets. Standard tablets act quickly and may need taking several times a day, while slow-release ones work gradually, so they are taken less often. The NHS says the prescriber sets the amount, and that treatment is usually started small and built up slowly to limit side effects. It says taking metformin with or just after a meal helps limit side effects, and that tablets are swallowed whole with water rather than chewed. For diabetes, the NHS says treatment is usually long term, and that stopping suddenly makes blood sugar rise. Because the NHS pages give different schedules for other uses, such as in children, the prescriber's instructions and the leaflet in the pack are the guide for any one person.

body.heading: What side effects are common, and do they settle?
body.body: The NHS lists nausea, being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain, loss of appetite and a change in taste among the common side effects. It says most of these should ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine, although some can last longer. The NHS says taking the tablets with a meal and building up slowly can reduce them. If they remain too much, it says a doctor may suggest slow-release tablets instead. Diabetes UK also says stomach-related effects often go away within a few weeks, and that side effects can happen at any time during treatment, not only at the start. Diabetes UK advises people on standard-release tablets who have these effects to talk to their GP or diabetes team.

body.heading: What about vitamin B12?
body.body: The NHS says that taking metformin for a long time can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, which can make a person very tired. Diabetes UK likewise says long-term use can lower vitamin B12 levels. The NHS says a doctor may check B12 levels in the blood, and that vitamin B12 supplements help if levels are too low. Symptoms mentioned alongside deficiency include tiredness, muscle weakness and a sore, red tongue.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about illness, dehydration, alcohol and scans?
body.body: The NHS says that being ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or a high temperature while taking metformin carries a risk of dehydration, meaning the body loses too much water. Other NHS guidance in the results says metformin may need to be paused during such illness and that the GP should be contacted. On alcohol, the NHS says drinking is possible while taking metformin, but gives limits, because drinking more can raise the risk of low blood sugar. An NHS trust leaflet adds that heavy drinking may raise the risk of lactic acidosis. The NHS says metformin may need to be stopped before surgery under general anaesthetic and before scans or tests that use an injected dye. It says the doctor will tell a person when to restart.

body.heading: Who may not be able to take metformin?
body.body: The NHS says most adults and children aged 10 and over can take metformin, but it is not suitable for everyone. Situations to raise with a doctor before starting include a past allergic reaction to metformin, liver or kidney problems, a severe infection, heart failure or a recent heart attack, and heavy alcohol use. The NHS says metformin can be taken in pregnancy, alone or with insulin, and usually while breastfeeding, after checking with a doctor. It also says there is no evidence that metformin reduces fertility in men or women.

body.heading: What if a dose is missed, or serious symptoms appear?
body.body: The NHS says not to take two doses to make up for a missed one. A pharmacist or GP is the usual route for questions about a missed dose or about side effects that do not settle. Lactic acidosis is a rare but serious side effect, and the NHS lists being sick, stomach pain, muscle cramps and breathing problems as signs. The NHS says to call 999 for suspected lactic acidosis or a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis). For other serious side effects, it says to call NHS 111. NHS 111 is also the NHS route if more than the prescribed amount has been taken.
